knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4.8, out.width = "100%", dpi = 96)
# Cut each figure to a palette of 256 colours, about a third of its size with
# no visible change, because the built vignettes ship in the tarball
if (requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE)) {
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.process = function(path) {
    img <- magick::image_quantize(magick::image_read(path), max = 256,
                                  colorspace = "sRGB", dither = FALSE)
    magick::image_write(img, path, format = "png")

**detfield** turns the detections of a fixed receiver array into hourly location surfaces:
for each tagged animal and hour, the probability that it was in each water cell. It reads the
range model you fitted to your range test, measures distances through water round points and
islands, and builds a detection field that gives every receiver a probability of hearing a
transmission from every cell. The surfaces then use every listening receiver, the silent ones
included. This page runs the whole chain on the Stoney Lake example included with the package:
a range test, 70 receivers on a 100 m raster, and five simulated animals with known tracks
over 48 hours from 1 June 2024.

Four articles go further. [Range models: bring your own, or start from two
distances](range-model.html) takes a range model that varies with depth and date into a
field for each day. [Hourly positions against the true track](positioning.html) scores the
surfaces against the simulated tracks, from the hourly error to the use map. [Habitat
selection: depth use from hourly positions](habitat-selection.html) draws availability
points and compares the depth coefficient from positions with the one from the true tracks.
[Position fish from a cleaned detection set](from-detqc.html) hands a cleaned detection
set from the [**detqc**](https://jakebrownscombe.github.io/detqc/) R package to
**detfield**.

## 1. Read the range test and count it

A range test is three files: the receivers, the range-test tags with their positions and
delays, and the detections. Serial numbers are read as text, so that leading zeros survive.

```{r read-range-test}
# Attach detfield, and ggplot2 for the figures
library(detfield)
library(ggplot2)
# Find a file included with the package
in_file <- function(name) system.file("extdata", name, package = "detfield")
serial_text <- c(receiver_serial = "character")
# Read the three range-test files and count their rows
rt_detections <- read.csv(in_file("stoney_range_test_detections.csv"),
                          colClasses = serial_text)
rt_receivers <- read.csv(in_file("stoney_range_test_receivers.csv"),
                         colClasses = serial_text)
rt_tags <- read.csv(in_file("stoney_range_test_tags.csv"))
c(detections = nrow(rt_detections), receivers = nrow(rt_receivers),
  tags = nrow(rt_tags))
```

The times are text in the files; **detfield** takes them as date-times in UTC:

```{r range-test-times}
# Convert detection, deployment and recovery times to UTC date-times
rt_detections$datetime <- as.POSIXct(rt_detections$datetime, tz = "UTC")
for (col in c("deploy_datetime", "recover_datetime")) {
  rt_receivers[[col]] <- as.POSIXct(rt_receivers[[col]], tz = "UTC")
  rt_tags[[col]] <- as.POSIXct(rt_tags[[col]], tz = "UTC")
}
range(rt_detections$datetime)
```

`range_test_counts()` returns one row per receiver, tag and whole hour in which both were in
the water: the transmissions sent, the detections heard, the distance and the receiver depth.
Hours in which a receiver heard nothing from a tag stay in, with `heard = 0`.

```{r count-range-test}
# Count transmissions sent and heard per receiver, tag and hour
range_test <- range_test_counts(rt_detections, rt_receivers, rt_tags)
head(range_test[, c("datetime", "depth_m", "distance_m", "sent", "heard")])
# Count the rows per receiver depth (m) and distance (m)
table(range_test$depth_m, range_test$distance_m)
```

## 2. Fit the range model

**detfield** never fits a range model; it reads yours. The range model here is a logistic
regression of the transmissions heard on distance, receiver depth and their interaction, so
that a deeper receiver hears further. Its Pearson dispersion measures spread beyond the
binomial:

```{r fit-range-model}
# Fit a binomial GLM of heard out of sent on distance and receiver depth
fit <- glm(cbind(heard, sent - heard) ~ distance_m * depth_m,
           family = binomial, data = range_test)
# Compute the Pearson dispersion: near 1 means no spread beyond the binomial
dispersion <- sum(residuals(fit, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(fit)
dispersion
```

A dispersion of `r round(dispersion, 2)` is consistent with no variation between receivers or
hours beyond binomial chance, so the model below takes the spread as 0. `de_model()` wraps the
fit with that spread:

```{r de-model}
# Wrap the fitted model with a spread of 0
model <- de_model(fit, sigma = list(station_hour = 0))
model
```

```{r plot-range-model, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Fitted detection curves at 1 m and 25 m receiver depth over the share of transmissions heard at each distance; the curve reaches further at 25 m."}
# Predict the fitted curve every 10 m at the two tested depths
curves <- expand.grid(distance_m = seq(0, 1600, by = 10), depth_m = c(1, 25))
curves$p <- plogis(model$predict(curves$distance_m, depth_m = curves$depth_m))
# Pool the share heard at each depth and distance over hours
pooled <- aggregate(cbind(heard, sent) ~ depth_m + distance_m,
                    data = range_test, FUN = sum)
# Plot the curves over the pooled shares
ggplot(curves, aes(distance_m, p, colour = factor(depth_m))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = pooled, aes(y = heard / sent), shape = 21,
             fill = "white", size = 2.4, stroke = 1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Receiver depth (m)", end = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Distance (m)", y = "Detection probability per transmission") +
  theme_positionr()
```

*The fitted model (lines) over the share of transmissions heard at each distance (open
points), pooled over the `r length(unique(range_test$datetime[range_test$depth_m == 1]))` hours
the test ran at each depth.*

A study with tag models, changing conditions or receiver effects fits a richer model; [Range
models: bring your own, or start from two distances](range-model.html) takes one with depth
and date into a field for each day.

## 3. Build the detection field

The field needs the lake raster, with land as `NA`, and the receiver deployments:

```{r read-lake}
# Read the depth raster of the lake
lake <- terra::rast(in_file("stoney_depth.tif"))
# Read the receiver deployments and convert their times to UTC
deployments <- read.csv(in_file("stoney_deployments.csv"),
                        colClasses = serial_text)
for (col in c("deploy_datetime", "recover_datetime")) {
  deployments[[col]] <- as.POSIXct(deployments[[col]], tz = "UTC")
}
nrow(deployments)
```

`water_distances()` measures the distance through water from each receiver to each water cell,
going round land. It reads the receiver positions from `deploy_lat` and `deploy_lon`.

```{r water-distances}
# Measure the distance through water from each receiver to each water cell
distances <- water_distances(lake, deployments)
distances
```

`de_field()` reads the model at each distance and at each receiver's own depth, `deploy_z`:

```{r field}
# Compute the detection probability per receiver and water cell
field <- de_field(distances, model)
field
```

`plot()` maps the probability that at least one receiver detects a transmission from each
cell:

```{r plot-field, fig.height = 5.2, fig.alt = "Probability that at least one of the 70 receivers detects a transmission from each water cell of Stoney Lake: bright overlapping patches round the receivers, darker water between and beyond them."}
# Map the field: the probability that any receiver detects a transmission
plot(field)
```

*Probability that at least one of the `r ncol(field$p)` receivers (rings) detects one
transmission from each of the `r format(nrow(field$p), big.mark = ",")` water cells.*

## 4. Compute the hourly location surfaces

The animals' detections and their tags are two more files:

```{r read-detections}
# Read the detections and convert their times to UTC
detections <- read.csv(in_file("stoney_detections.csv"),
                       colClasses = serial_text)
detections$datetime <- as.POSIXct(detections$datetime, tz = "UTC")
# Read the tags and their delays
tags <- read.csv(in_file("stoney_tags.csv"))
tags
```

`bin_detections()` counts, for each animal and hour with a detection, the detections at every
receiver that was listening, the silent ones included, and the transmissions the tag sent
(`n`, from its delay):

```{r bin-detections}
# Count detections per animal, hour and listening receiver
counts <- bin_detections(detections, deployments, tags)
head(counts[counts$y > 0, c("animal_id", "bin_start", "station_id", "y", "n")])
# Count the detected hours per animal
table(unique(counts[c("animal_id", "bin_start")])$animal_id)
```

`location_surface()` computes, for each animal and detected hour, the probability that the
animal was in each water cell, from the counts at every listening receiver. Each hour is
computed on its own, with no movement model linking hours
([the model](positioning.html#the-model)).

```{r location-surface}
# Compute one surface per animal and detected hour
surface <- location_surface(counts, field)
surface
```

The print gives the cells kept per hour, the hours whose counts no single cell explains
(`Misfit`), and the hours placed on a ring away from the receiver that heard most (`Near`),
which happens when an hour is heard mostly by one receiver. In the hour from 07:00 UTC on 1 June 2024,
four receivers heard `stoney-01`. Its surface for that hour is drawn with its true path from
the simulation:

```{r one-hour}
# Select the counts, at the receivers that heard it, from 07:00 UTC
hour_start <- as.POSIXct("2024-06-01 07:00:00", tz = "UTC")
hour_counts <- counts[counts$animal_id == "stoney-01" &
                        counts$bin_start == hour_start, ]
hour_counts[hour_counts$y > 0, c("station_id", "y", "n")]
# Select the true path of the hour, one position a minute
true_path <- stoney_track$track
true_path <- true_path[true_path$animal_id == "stoney-01" &
                         true_path$datetime >= hour_start &
                         true_path$datetime <= hour_start + 3600, ]
nrow(true_path)
```

```{r plot-surface, fig.height = 4.8, fig.alt = "Location surface of stoney-01 for one hour: a compact bright patch between the four receivers that heard it, with its 50% and 95% credible regions outlined and the true path running through it."}
# Map the surface, with the true path drawn on a white edge
plot(surface, animal_id = "stoney-01", bin_start = hour_start) +
  geom_path(data = true_path, aes(x, y), colour = "white", linewidth = 1.6,
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_path(data = true_path, aes(x, y), colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.8,
            inherit.aes = FALSE)
```

*Location surface of `stoney-01` for 07:00 to 08:00 UTC on 1 June 2024, with the true path of
the hour (line, one position a minute).*

The surface lies where the four ranges meet, pulled away from the silent receivers round it.
[Hourly positions against the true track](positioning.html) shows every hour of one animal
this way and scores all five against their tracks.

## 5. Summarise with credible regions and draws

`credible_region()` returns each hour's smallest set of cells holding 95% of the probability,
with its area:

```{r credible-region}
# Find the 95% region of every hour, and its area
regions <- credible_region(surface, level = 0.95)
region_areas <- attr(regions, "summary")
# Compute the median area of the 95% region per animal, in ha
aggregate(list(median_ha = region_areas$area_m2 / 1e4),
          by = region_areas["animal_id"], FUN = function(ha) round(median(ha)))
```

`sample_locations()` draws cells from each surface in proportion to their probability, for
analyses that take points, such as habitat selection. The draws describe the hours in which
the animal was detected, and only those.

```{r sample-locations}
# Draw 20 cells per detected hour in proportion to probability
draws <- sample_locations(surface, n = 20, seed = 1)
head(draws, 3)
attr(draws, "estimand")
```

```{r plot-draws, fig.height = 5.4, dpi = 110, fig.alt = "Map of Stoney Lake with the draws of the five animals as points, one set per animal, and each true track as a line through its draws."}
# Turn depth to metres below the surface (the raster stores it as negative)
depth_cells <- terra::as.data.frame(abs(lake), xy = TRUE)
names(depth_cells)[3] <- "depth_m"
# Warm colours, which read on the blue depth ramp, one per animal; each
# track is a darker shade of its animal's colour, so it can be followed
# through its own draws
animals <- sort(unique(draws$animal_id))
draw_colours <- setNames(c("#FF8C00", "#FF3B3B", "#FF66CC", "#FFE135",
                           "#B3FF00"), animals)
track_colours <- grDevices::rgb(t(grDevices::col2rgb(draw_colours)) * 0.55,
                                maxColorValue = 255)
names(track_colours) <- animals
# Draw each animal's track thin, in its own dark shade
track_layers <- lapply(animals, function(a) {
  geom_path(data = stoney_track$track[stoney_track$track$animal_id == a, ],
            colour = track_colours[[a]], linewidth = 0.25)
})
# Map the depth, the draws, the tracks over them, then the receivers
ggplot(depth_cells, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = depth_m)) +
  scale_fill_depth() +
  geom_point(data = draws, aes(colour = animal_id), alpha = 0.6, size = 1.3,
             stroke = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Animal", values = draw_colours) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2.6))) +
  track_layers +
  layer_receivers(attr(distances, "receivers"), size = 1.2,
                  stroke = 0.45) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Easting (m, UTM 17N)", y = "Northing (m, UTM 17N)") +
  annotation_scale_bar(location = "br") +
  theme_positionr()
```

*Positions of the five simulated animals over 1 and 2 June 2024: 20 cells drawn from each
detected hour's surface (`r format(nrow(draws), big.mark = ",")` draws, many on the same cell),
with the true tracks (lines, one position a minute) and the `r nrow(deployments)` receivers
(rings).*

Most of each animal's draws sit along its own track. The draws of single-receiver hours sit on
arcs round the receiver that heard the animal, some of them away from the track, as in the
north-west arm, the north-east basin and the middle basin. [Hourly positions against the true
track](positioning.html) scores the positions and writes draws like these to files for other
packages.
